questions.q: In a sundial, the time of day is found from:
questions.a: The changing position of the shadow of an object cast by sunlight. The chapter says that in a sundial time is determined by the changing position of the shadow cast by the light of the Sun.
o: The changing position of the shadow of an object cast by sunlight
The level of water left in a vessel
The flow of sand from one bulb to another
The length of a marked candle that has burnt

questions.q: Early humans noticed that many events in nature repeat after definite intervals. Which of these was used to define a day?
questions.a: The cycle of rising and setting of the Sun. The chapter says a day was defined by the cycle of rising and setting of the Sun.
o: The cycle of rising and setting of the Sun
The burning of a candle clock

questions.q: Match each timekeeping device in Column I with what changes in it to show the passage of time in Column II. Column I: 1. Sundial; 2. Floating bowl-type water clock; 3. Hourglass; 4. Candle clock. Column II: (p) the position of a shadow cast by sunlight; (q) a bowl with a fine hole at the bottom fills up and sinks; (r) sand flows from one bulb to another; (s) a marked candle burns down past its markings.
questions.a: 1-p, 2-q, 3-r, 4-s: a sundial uses the moving shadow, the floating bowl fills and sinks in a fixed time, an hourglass uses sand flowing between bulbs, and a candle clock uses markings on a burning candle.

questions.q: Name the two types of water clock described in the chapter, and state in one line how each one measures time.
questions.a: (i) The water flowing out type: water flows out of a vessel that has markings for time. (ii) The floating bowl type: a bowl with a fine hole at the bottom floats on water, gradually fills up in a fixed time and sinks.
s: Water flowing out type: water flows out of a vessel marked for time
Floating bowl type: a bowl with a fine hole floats, fills in a fixed time and sinks

questions.q: Ritu makes the simple water clock of Activity 8.1 from a used plastic bottle. (a) What does she use to make the small hole in the cap? (b) How does she place the upper part of the bottle on the lower part? (c) Why does she add a few drops of ink to the water? (d) While making the clock, how often does she mark the water level? (e) Later she pours the water back into the top and starts a game. The water level touches three of her marks before the game ends. How long did the game last?
questions.a: (a) A drawing pin. (b) The upper part is placed upside down (inverted) over the lower half. (c) The ink makes the water level easy to see. (d) She marks the level after every one minute, using a watch, until all the water drips down. (e) Each mark reached means one more minute has passed, so the game lasted about 3 minutes.
s: (a) A drawing pin
(b) Inverted over the lower half
(c) To make the water level easily visible
(d) After every one minute, using a watch
(e) Three marks reached, so about 3 minutes

questions.q: Assertion (A): A sundial cannot be used to tell the time at night. Reason (R): In a sundial, time is found from the shadow of an object cast by the light of the Sun. Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: a sundial works only with the shadow made by sunlight, and there is no sunlight at night, so there is no shadow to read.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: Ritu makes the bottle water clock of Activity 8.1. She marks the water level after every one minute using a watch, and all the water drips down in 6 minutes. Consider these statements. I. In one run, her clock can measure at most about 6 minutes. II. If she adds more drops of ink to the water, her minute marks will come further apart. III. Her clock is set up by comparing it with another timekeeper. Which of these statements are correct?
questions.a: I and III only. The water runs out after 6 minutes, so one run times at most about 6 minutes; the marks were made by checking a watch, so the clock is set up against another timekeeper. The ink only makes the water level easy to see; it does not change how fast the water drips, so statement II is wrong.

questions.q: A trekking group camps for some days on a hillside with no clocks, watches or phones. For each need below, name one way or device from the chapter that they could use and give the reason. (i) Keeping count of how many days they have stayed. (ii) Knowing the time of day around noon on a bright, sunny day. (iii) Planning a night walk for the next full-moon night, which is some weeks away.
questions.a: (i) Count the cycles of the rising and setting of the Sun, because a day is defined by this cycle. (ii) A sundial, because on a sunny day the moving shadow of an object shows the time. (iii) Watch the phases of the Moon, because they repeat after a definite interval and were used by early humans for keeping track of time and making calendars.
s: (i) Count the rising and setting of the Sun, since this cycle defines a day
(ii) A sundial, which reads the time from a shadow in sunlight
(iii) Follow the phases of the Moon, a cycle that repeats after a definite interval

questions.q: A night watchman in an old fort must announce every hour from 8 pm to 2 am. He has three timers: a candle clock 20 cm long that burns steadily at 3 cm every hour and is marked every 3 cm; an hourglass whose sand runs out in 15 minutes; and a floating bowl that sinks every 24 minutes after it is floated. (a) Will the candle last the whole duty? Show the working. (b) How many times will the hourglass run out during the duty? (c) How many times will the bowl sink during the duty, and will one of its sinkings fall exactly at 9 pm? (d) Which timer lets him announce each hour with the fewest actions during the night (turning, refloating or relighting)? Give the reason. (e) If he lights the candle at 8 pm, how many centimetres of it are left at 2 am, and how many marks has it burnt past?
questions.a: (a) The duty lasts 6 h. The candle lasts 20 / 3 = 6 2/3 h = 6 h 40 min, so yes, it lasts the whole duty. (b) 6 h = 360 min, and 360 / 15 = 24 times. (c) 360 / 24 = 15 sinkings. At 9 pm only 60 min have passed and 60 / 24 = 2.5, so no sinking falls at 9 pm. (d) The candle clock: once lit it needs no action, and each 3 cm mark burns away in exactly one hour. The hourglass must be turned over after every run (24 runs, four for each hour), and the bowl must be refloated after every sinking and does not line up with the hours. (e) In 6 h it burns 6 x 3 = 18 cm, so 20 - 18 = 2 cm is left, and it has burnt past the marks at 3, 6, 9, 12, 15 and 18 cm, that is 6 marks.
s: (a) 20 / 3 = 6 h 40 min, more than the 6 h duty
(c) 360 / 24 = 15 sinkings; 60 / 24 = 2.5, so none at 9 pm
(d) Candle clock: no turning or refloating, one mark per hour
(e) 18 cm burnt, 2 cm left; 6 marks passed

questions.q: A school camp in a hill village has no electricity. The camp has three timers: a sundial in the open courtyard, a floating bowl-type water clock whose bowl fills and sinks 20 min after it is floated, and an hourglass whose sand runs out in 5 min. The camp holds a 40 min drawing class in the sunny courtyard at 11 am and a 20 min story session at 6 pm in a closed hall where no sunlight reaches. (a) Which timer cannot be used for the story session? Give the reason. (b) What must be done each time the bowl sinks, and each time the sand of the hourglass has all run down? (c) How many times in all must the bowl be floated to time the drawing class? (d) For the story session the leader wants the timer that needs no action from anyone once it is started until the session ends. Should she choose the floating bowl or the hourglass? Give the reason.
questions.a: (a) The sundial: it shows time only by the shadow cast by sunlight, and no sunlight reaches the hall at 6 pm. (b) The sunken bowl must be lifted up and floated again; the hourglass must be turned over so that the sand flows from one bulb to the other again. (c) 40 / 20 = 2 times (once at the start and once again when it sinks after 20 min). (d) The floating bowl: it sinks exactly once, at the end of the 20 min, so nothing has to be done during the session. The hourglass runs out every 5 min, so it would have to be turned over 3 times during the session (20 / 5 = 4 runs).
s: (a) Sundial: needs the shadow from sunlight; none in the hall
(b) Bowl lifted and floated again; hourglass turned over
(c) 40 / 20 = 2 times
(d) Floating bowl: sinks once, at 20 min; hourglass needs turning 3 times

questions.q: The world's largest stone sundial, the Samrat Yantra, is found at:
questions.a: Jantar Mantar, Jaipur. The chapter says the Samrat Yantra was built around 300 years ago at the Jantar Mantar in Jaipur, Rajasthan.

questions.q: The bowl of a Ghatika-yantra took 24 minutes to fill and sink, and this interval was called a ghatika or ghati. Into how many equal ghatis was a 24-hour day divided?
questions.a: 60. A day has 24 x 60 = 1440 minutes, and 1440 / 24 = 60 ghatis, as the chapter states.

questions.q: (a) Why were water clocks with water flowing out not very accurate? (b) Name the water clock that was developed because of this.
questions.a: (a) As the water level dropped, the flow rate of water decreased, so the clock did not mark time evenly. (b) The sinking bowl water clock, the Ghatika-yantra.
s: (a) The flow rate decreased as the water level dropped
(b) The sinking bowl water clock (Ghatika-yantra)

questions.q: Read about Galileo in the church and answer. (a) What caught Galileo's attention while he sat in the church? (b) What did he use to measure time? (c) After experimenting with different pendulums, what did he conclude?
questions.a: (a) A lamp hanging from the ceiling that was swinging back and forth. (b) His own pulse. (c) The time taken to complete one oscillation is always the same for a pendulum of a given length.
s: (a) A lamp hanging from the ceiling, swinging back and forth
(b) His pulse
(c) A pendulum of a given length always takes the same time for one oscillation

questions.q: State True or False and give the reason: 'Galileo Galilei invented the pendulum clock in 1656.'
questions.a: False. The pendulum clock was invented in 1656 by Christiaan Huygens; Huygens was inspired by Galileo's investigations of pendulums.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: Christiaan Huygens invented it in 1656, inspired by Galileo's study of pendulums

questions.q: Assertion (A): The Ghatika-yantra continued to be used at religious places for rituals. Reason (R): The Ghatika-yantra was progressively replaced by pendulum clocks in the late nineteenth century. Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A: R tells us that pendulum clocks took over its general use in the late nineteenth century; it does not explain why the Ghatika-yantra was still kept for rituals at religious places.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: Match each name in Column I with the contribution to timekeeping in Column II. Column I: 1. The Arthasastra by Kautilya; 2. Varahamihira; 3. Aryabhata; 4. Christiaan Huygens. Column II: (p) the earliest reference to shadow-based time measurement; (q) an accurate expression for time in terms of the shadow of a vertical stick, around 530 CE; (r) the first mention of the sinking bowl water clock; (s) the pendulum clock, invented in 1656.
questions.a: 1-p, 2-q, 3-r, 4-s: the Arthasastra has the earliest reference to shadow-based timekeeping, Varahamihira gave the shadow expression around 530 CE, Aryabhata first mentioned the Ghatika-yantra, and Huygens invented the pendulum clock in 1656.

questions.q: The ghati measured by the Ghatika-yantra became the standard unit of time in ancient India, while the water clock with water flowing out never gave such a unit. Which reason from the chapter best explains this?
o: The hole in each bowl was made so that it took 24 minutes to fill and sink, so every sinking marked the same interval
The Ghatika-yantra used the shadow of the Sun, which is the same in every town
The bowl of a Ghatika-yantra sank faster as the water level around it dropped
The Ghatika-yantra needed no one to lift the bowl and float it again
questions.a: The hole in each bowl was made so that it took 24 minutes to fill and sink, so every sinking marked the same interval. In the outflow clock the flow rate decreased as the water level dropped, so its intervals were not even and it was not very accurate.

questions.q: Kabir writes in his notebook: 'Before modern clocks, people in India could tell time only by shadows, so after sunset they had no way of measuring time.' Use the chapter to check his claim.
questions.a: The claim is wrong. In ancient India time was measured using both shadows and water clocks. The Ghatika-yantra (sinking bowl water clock) needed no sunlight; it was used to measure time constantly at monasteries, palaces and town squares, and each sinking was announced by drums, conch shells or a gong, so time was kept after sunset too.
s: Verdict: the claim is wrong
Ancient India measured time with water clocks as well as shadows
The Ghatika-yantra needs no sunlight and kept time constantly, its sinkings announced by drums, conches or gongs

questions.q: An old palace record gives the length of its daily events in ghatis, the unit measured by the Ghatika-yantra, whose bowl took 24 minutes to fill and sink. The morning court lasts 2.5 ghatis, the midday feast 5 ghatis and the evening lamp lighting 3.75 ghatis. A student is preparing a museum notice board in hours and minutes, and the museum also wants to add a music programme of 2 h 24 min. (a) How many ghatis make one hour? (b) Write the length of each of the three events in hours and minutes. (c) How many ghatis long is the music programme? (d) The museum is open for 7 h a day. Can all four events be shown one after another in one day? Show the working in ghatis.
questions.a: (a) One hour = 60 min and one ghati = 24 min, so 60 / 24 = 2.5 ghatis make one hour. (b) Court: 2.5 x 24 = 60 min = 1 h; feast: 5 x 24 = 120 min = 2 h; lamp lighting: 3.75 x 24 = 90 min = 1 h 30 min. (c) 2 h 24 min = 144 min, and 144 / 24 = 6 ghatis. (d) The events total 2.5 + 5 + 3.75 + 6 = 17.25 ghatis. The museum is open 7 h = 420 min = 420 / 24 = 17.5 ghatis, so yes, they fit, with 0.25 ghati (6 min) to spare.
s: (b) 1 h, 2 h and 1 h 30 min
(c) 144 / 24 = 6 ghatis
(d) 17.25 ghatis needed, 17.5 available: yes, 6 min to spare

questions.q: In a simple pendulum, the small metallic ball hung from the thread is called the:
questions.a: Bob. The chapter calls the small metallic ball of a simple pendulum the bob.

questions.q: A simple pendulum takes 16 s to complete 10 oscillations. What is its time period?
questions.a: 1.6 s. The time period is the time for one oscillation: 16 s / 10 = 1.6 s.

questions.q: (a) What is the time period of a simple pendulum? (b) What is the position of a pendulum at rest called?
questions.a: (a) The time taken by the pendulum to complete one oscillation. (b) The mean position.
s: (a) Time taken to complete one oscillation
(b) Mean position

questions.q: State True or False and give the reason: 'The time period of a simple pendulum depends on the length of its thread.'
questions.a: True. The time period of a simple pendulum depends on its length, but it does not depend on the mass of the bob.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: the time period depends on the length but not on the mass of the bob

questions.q: In the school lab, Farhan ties a stone to a thread and hangs it from a rigid support so that the thread is 100 cm long. He waits for the stone to come to rest, then moves it slightly to one side and releases it without pushing. Using a watch, he finds that it completes 15 oscillations in 30 s, and he gets the same result each time he repeats the timing. (a) What is the position of the pendulum at rest called? (b) Find the time period of his pendulum. (c) How many oscillations will it complete in 1 min? (d) Which property of a pendulum makes it useful for measuring time?
questions.a: (a) The mean position. (b) Time period = 30 s / 15 = 2 s. (c) 1 min = 60 s, and 60 / 2 = 30 oscillations. (d) The time period of a simple pendulum of a given length is constant at a place.
s: (a) Mean position
(c) 60 / 2 = 30 oscillations
(d) Its time period for a given length is constant at a place

questions.q: Assertion (A): Two simple pendulums at the same place, each with an 80 cm thread, one with a 50 g bob and one with a 500 g bob, have almost the same time period. Reason (R): The time period of a simple pendulum depends on its length but not on the mass of its bob. Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: the two pendulums have the same length, and since the bob's mass does not affect the time period, their time periods are almost the same.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: In Activity 8.2 the time for 10 oscillations is measured with a watch and then divided by 10, instead of timing a single oscillation. What is the main advantage of doing this?
o: One oscillation is so short that a small delay in starting or stopping the watch would be a large part of it; over 10 oscillations the same delay is shared out
Dividing by 10 makes the time period of the pendulum smaller
The first oscillation always takes longer than the others, so it must be left out
A watch cannot show any time shorter than 10 s
questions.a: One oscillation is so short that a small delay in starting or stopping the watch would be a large part of it; over 10 oscillations the same delay is spread over all of them, so the time period found is more reliable. Dividing does not change the pendulum, and each oscillation takes almost the same time.

questions.q: Tara and Dev time the same simple pendulum in two different ways. Tara starts her stopwatch as the bob passes the mean position O moving towards the extreme position A, and counts one oscillation each time the bob is back at O moving towards A. Dev starts his stopwatch with the bob at the extreme position A and counts one oscillation each time the bob is back at A. (a) Write the path of the bob in one oscillation for Tara's way and for Dev's way. (b) Tara finds 10 oscillations take 18 s. About how long should Dev's stopwatch show for 10 oscillations, and why? (c) Why is the motion of the pendulum called periodic?
questions.a: (a) Tara: O to A, then to B, then back to O. Dev: A to B and back to A. (b) About 18 s. Both ways count one complete oscillation, so the time period is the same, 18 / 10 = 1.8 s, and 10 oscillations take about 18 s. (c) The bob repeats its path after a fixed interval of time.
s: (a) Tara O-A-B-O; Dev A-B-A
(b) About 18 s: both count a full oscillation, time period 1.8 s
(c) It repeats its path after a fixed interval of time

questions.q: Two simple pendulums hang side by side. Pendulum X has a time period of 1.2 s and pendulum Y has a time period of 1.8 s. Both bobs are pulled to the same extreme position A side and released together. (a) How many oscillations does each complete in 18 s? (b) After how many seconds will both bobs first be back at their starting positions together? (c) How many times will this happen in the first 36 s? (d) Where is the bob of X at 9 s after release: at its starting extreme position, at its mean position, or at its other extreme position? Give the reason.
questions.a: (a) X: 18 / 1.2 = 15 oscillations; Y: 18 / 1.8 = 10 oscillations. (b) X is back at the start at 1.2, 2.4, 3.6 s ...; Y at 1.8, 3.6 s ...; the first common time is 3.6 s (3 oscillations of X, 2 of Y). (c) 36 / 3.6 = 10 times. (d) At its other extreme position. In 9 s X completes 9 / 1.2 = 7.5 oscillations. After 7 complete oscillations it is back at its starting extreme position A; in the next half oscillation it moves from A to the other extreme position B, so at 9 s it is at B.
s: (a) X 15, Y 10 oscillations
(d) 9 / 1.2 = 7.5 oscillations, so the bob is at the other extreme position B

questions.q: The school's only watch stops during a science fair. Lata has two simple pendulums whose time periods she measured earlier: pendulum P, 1.5 s, and pendulum Q, 1.6 s. She will time events by counting oscillations. (a) A quiz round must last 3 min. How many oscillations of each pendulum make 3 min? (b) Which pendulum should she use for the quiz round? Give the reason. (c) A relay race must last 4 min. Can either pendulum be used for it? Show the working. (d) A balloon race lasted 45 oscillations of Q. How long was it, in minutes and seconds? (e) A friend shortens P's thread by tying a knot in it. Can Lata still count 1.5 s for each oscillation of P? Give the reason.
questions.a: (a) 3 min = 180 s. P: 180 / 1.5 = 120 oscillations; Q: 180 / 1.6 = 112.5 oscillations. (b) Pendulum P: 3 min is a whole number (120) of its oscillations, so she can stop exactly at the end of a count; with Q the quiz would end halfway through an oscillation, which is hard to judge. (c) 4 min = 240 s. P: 240 / 1.5 = 160; Q: 240 / 1.6 = 150. Both are whole numbers, so either pendulum can be used. (d) 45 x 1.6 = 72 s = 1 min 12 s. (e) No. The time period depends on the length of the pendulum, so after the thread is shortened she must measure P's time period again.
s: (a) P 120, Q 112.5 oscillations
(b) P: a whole number of oscillations
(c) P 160, Q 150: either can be used
(e) No: the length has changed, so the time period must be measured again

questions.q: The SI unit of time and its correct symbol are:
questions.a: Second, s. The chapter says the SI unit of time is the second and its symbol is s.

questions.q: Which of these is written correctly according to the rules for writing units of time?
questions.a: 45 min: the symbol is in lowercase and singular, has no full stop, and there is a space between the number and the unit.

questions.q: A bus journey lasts 2 h. How many seconds is that?

Consider these statements. I. Quartz clocks use tiny and very rapid vibrations of a quartz crystal. II. A millisecond is one-thousandth of a second. III. Atomic clocks keep time by the swinging of a long pendulum. Which of these statements are correct?
questions.a: I and II only. Quartz clocks use vibrations of a quartz crystal and a millisecond is one-thousandth of a second, but atomic clocks use vibrations from specific atoms, not a pendulum, so statement III is wrong.

questions.q: State True or False and give the reason: 'The time 15min on a notice should be written as 15 min.'
questions.a: True. While writing the time, a space is always left between the number and the unit, so it should be written 15 min.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: a space is left between the number and the unit

questions.q: Huygens' early pendulum clocks could gain or lose 10 seconds each day, while today's atomic clocks lose only one second in millions of years. Which comparison over one year (365 days) is correct?
o: An early pendulum clock could be off by up to about one hour, while an atomic clock would be off by far less than one second
An early pendulum clock could be off by only about 10 seconds, the same as an atomic clock
An early pendulum clock could be off by about one minute, while an atomic clock would be off by about one second
Both clocks could be off by about one hour
questions.a: An early pendulum clock could be off by up to about one hour, while an atomic clock would be off by far less than one second: 10 s x 365 = 3650 s, which is about 61 min, while an atomic clock loses only one second in millions of years.

questions.q: A notice on the school board reads: 'The drawing test lasts 1Hrs 30 Mins.' (a) Write the time correctly using the rules in the chapter. (b) Give two rules that the notice breaks.
questions.a: (a) 1 h 30 min. (b) Any two: 'hrs' is incorrect, the symbol for hour is h; symbols are written in lowercase, so not 'Mins'; symbols are written in singular, so 'min', not 'mins'; a space is left between the number and the unit.
s: (a) 1 h 30 min
(b) Two rules, e.g. 'hrs' is wrong (use h); symbols lowercase and singular; space between number and unit

questions.q: Assertion (A): A quartz clock works on the same basic principle as a pendulum clock. Reason (R): A quartz clock uses tiny and very rapid vibrations of a quartz crystal, which repeat periodically. Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: both clocks count a periodically repeating process; the quartz clock simply uses the rapid vibrations of a crystal instead of a swinging pendulum.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: (a) Arrange these intervals from the shortest to the longest: 1 s, 1 millisecond, 1 microsecond, one-hundredth of a second. (b) In a 100 m race the timer shows that the winner finished 0.04 s ahead of the runner-up. Write this gap in milliseconds. (c) An ECG machine reads the heart's signal once every 4 milliseconds. How many readings does it take in 1 s?
questions.a: (a) 1 microsecond, 1 millisecond, one-hundredth of a second, 1 s. (b) 1 s = 1000 milliseconds, so 0.04 s = 0.04 x 1000 = 40 milliseconds. (c) 1 s = 1000 milliseconds, so it takes 1000 / 4 = 250 readings in 1 s.
s: (a) microsecond, millisecond, hundredth of a second, second
(b) 0.04 x 1000 = 40 milliseconds
(c) 1000 / 4 = 250 readings

questions.q: A science club wants to choose a repeating process to use as a simple clock. They time five repeats of each process, one after another. A dripping tap: the gaps between drops are 2.0 s, 2.6 s, 1.7 s, 2.9 s and 2.3 s. A simple pendulum with a 100 cm thread: its oscillations take 2.0 s, 2.0 s, 2.1 s, 2.0 s and 2.0 s. A ball dropped once on the floor: the gaps between bounces are 1.2 s, 0.9 s, 0.7 s, 0.5 s and 0.3 s, and then it stops. (a) Which process cannot be used as a clock at all? Give the reason. (b) Find the difference between the longest and the shortest interval for the tap and for the pendulum. (c) Which process should the club choose? Justify using the principle on which all clocks work. (d) Taking each repeat of the chosen process as 2.0 s, how many repeats make 1 min? (e) Give one reason why quartz and atomic clocks keep time far better than a pendulum clock.
questions.a: (a) The bouncing ball: its gaps keep getting shorter and it soon stops, so it is not a process that repeats continuously at equal intervals. (b) Tap: 2.9 - 1.7 = 1.2 s; pendulum: 2.1 - 2.0 = 0.1 s. (c) The pendulum. All clocks are based on a process that repeats continuously to mark equal intervals of time, and the pendulum's intervals are almost equal (a spread of only 0.1 s against 1.2 s for the tap). (d) 1 min = 60 s, and 60 / 2.0 = 30 repeats. (e) They use tiny and very rapid vibrations of a quartz crystal or of specific atoms; Huygens' early pendulum clocks could gain or lose 10 seconds a day, while atomic clocks lose only one second in millions of years.
s: (a) The ball: gaps shrink and it stops, so it does not repeat at equal intervals
(b) Tap 1.2 s, pendulum 0.1 s
(c) Pendulum: nearly equal intervals, as a clock needs a steadily repeating process
(d) 60 / 2.0 = 30 repeats
(e) Very rapid vibrations of a quartz crystal or atoms; far smaller error than 10 s a day

questions.q: What is the SI unit of speed?
questions.a: Metre per second (m/s). Speed is distance divided by time, so its SI unit is metre/second, written m/s.

questions.q: A boy runs 60 m in 12 s. What is his speed?
questions.a: 5 m/s. Speed = total distance / total time = 60 m / 12 s = 5 m/s.

questions.q: In a race on a straight track, all runners start together. Ten seconds after the start, Ravi has covered 55 m, Ali 60 m and Joy 48 m. Who is running the fastest?
questions.a: Ali. In the same time, the one who has covered the most distance is the fastest, and Ali has covered 60 m.

questions.q: A car moves at a speed of 60 km/h. (a) How far does it go in 3 h? (b) How long does it take to cover 240 km?
questions.a: (a) Distance = speed x time = 60 km/h x 3 h = 180 km. (b) Time = distance / speed = 240 km / 60 km/h = 4 h.

questions.q: Kiran walks 2.4 km to the library in 40 min. (a) Write the formula for speed. (b) Find her speed in km/h. (c) Find her speed in m/s.
questions.a: (a) Speed = total distance covered / total time taken. (b) 40 min = 2/3 h, so speed = 2.4 km / (2/3 h) = 3.6 km/h. (c) 2.4 km = 2400 m and 40 min = 2400 s, so speed = 2400 m / 2400 s = 1 m/s.
s: (a) Speed = total distance / total time

questions.q: State True or False and give the reason: 'An ostrich running at 12 m/s is faster than a scooter moving at 45 km/h.'
questions.a: False. 45 km/h = 45 x 1000 m / 3600 s = 12.5 m/s, and 12 m/s is less than 12.5 m/s, so the scooter is faster.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: 45 km/h = 12.5 m/s, which is more than 12 m/s

questions.q: Assertion (A): An athlete who runs 200 m in 25 s is faster than one who runs 100 m in 13 s. Reason (R): An athlete who covers a greater distance is always the faster one. Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false: the first athlete's speed is 200 / 25 = 8 m/s and the second's is 100 / 13, about 7.7 m/s, so A is true; but speed depends on the distance covered in unit time, not on the total distance alone, so R is false.
o: A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: A goods train moves at a speed of 20 m/s. How long does it take to cover 36 km?
questions.a: 30 min. 36 km = 36000 m, and time = distance / speed = 36000 m / 20 m/s = 1800 s = 30 min.

questions.q: Meera leaves home at 8:00 am for an exam centre 12 km away and must reach by 8:36 am. She has four choices: walk at 1.5 m/s; cycle at 18 km/h; wait 8 min for an auto and then ride at 30 km/h; or wait 18 min for a bus and then ride at 36 km/h. (a) Express her walking speed in km/h. (b) Find the total time for each choice. (c) Which choices get her there in time? (d) At what speed would she have to cycle to arrive exactly at 8:36 am? (e) Which choice should she take? Give the reason.
questions.a: (a) 1.5 m/s = 1.5 x 3600 / 1000 = 5.4 km/h. (b) Walk: 12 / 5.4 h = 133 min 20 s; cycle: 12 / 18 h = 40 min; auto: 8 + (12 / 30 x 60) = 8 + 24 = 32 min; bus: 18 + (12 / 36 x 60) = 18 + 20 = 38 min. (c) She has 36 min, so only the auto (32 min) gets her there in time. (d) Speed = 12 km / (36/60 h) = 20 km/h. (e) The auto, because it is the only choice that reaches within 36 min, even with the 8-minute wait.
s: (a) 5.4 km/h
(b) Walk 133 min 20 s, cycle 40 min, auto 32 min, bus 38 min
(c) Only the auto
(e) The auto, the only choice within 36 min

questions.q: Class 7 goes on a school trip by bus, and the class monitor keeps a log. The bus leaves the school at 7:40 am and reaches a lake 60 km away at 9:20 am. It halts at the lake for 20 min, then leaves for a hill fort 30 km further on and reaches it at 11:00 am. (a) Find the time taken for each part of the journey. (b) Find the speed of the bus in km/h on each part. (c) Express the higher of the two speeds in m/s. (d) On which part did the bus move faster, by the rule in the chapter? Find its average speed for the whole trip from the school to the fort, counting the halt.
questions.a: (a) School to lake: 7:40 am to 9:20 am = 1 h 40 min; lake to fort: it leaves at 9:40 am, so 9:40 am to 11:00 am = 1 h 20 min. (b) School to lake: 60 / (5/3) = 36 km/h; lake to fort: 30 / (4/3) = 22.5 km/h. (c) 36 km/h = 36 x 1000 m / 3600 s = 10 m/s. (d) School to lake, because it covered more distance in unit time (36 km/h against 22.5 km/h). Whole trip: 90 km in 3 h 20 min = 10/3 h, so average speed = 90 / (10/3) = 27 km/h.
s: (a) 1 h 40 min and 1 h 20 min
(b) 36 km/h and 22.5 km/h
(d) School to lake is faster; average 90 / (10/3) = 27 km/h

questions.q: An object moving along a straight line with a constant speed is said to be in:
questions.a: Uniform linear motion. The chapter defines uniform linear motion as motion along a straight line with a constant speed.

questions.q: Which instrument fitted in a scooter records the distance travelled by the vehicle in kilometres?
questions.a: Odometer. The chapter says the odometer measures the distance travelled by the vehicle in kilometre, while the speedometer shows its speed.

questions.q: A cart moves along a straight road. Which set of distances, covered in successive 1-minute intervals, shows uniform linear motion?
questions.a: 50 m, 50 m, 50 m, 50 m. In uniform linear motion an object covers equal distances in equal intervals of time.

questions.q: (a) What is linear motion? (b) Give the example of linear motion used in the chapter.
questions.a: (a) When an object moves along a straight line, its motion is called linear motion. (b) A train moving on a straight track between two adjacent railway stations.
s: (a) Motion of an object along a straight line
(b) A train on a straight track between two adjacent stations

questions.q: A train leaves station A slowly, speeds up till point B, moves at a constant speed from B to C, and then slows down and stops at station D, all on a straight track. State the type of motion of the train (a) between A and B, (b) between B and C, (c) between C and D.
questions.a: (a) Non-uniform linear motion, because its speed is changing. (b) Uniform linear motion, because it moves at a constant speed. (c) Non-uniform linear motion, because its speed is changing as it slows down.
s: (a) A to B: non-uniform, speed changing
(b) B to C: uniform, constant speed
(c) C to D: non-uniform, slowing down

questions.q: Consider these statements. I. Uniform linear motion is common in everyday life, even over long distances. II. To find how far a car went on a trip, the odometer reading at the start is subtracted from the reading at the end. III. A train in uniform linear motion at 120 km/h covers 20 km in every 15 minutes. Which of these statements are correct?
questions.a: II only. The odometer records the distance travelled, so the difference of its readings is the distance of the trip. Uniform linear motion is an idealisation and is seldom seen over long distances in everyday life, so statement I is wrong. At 120 km/h a train covers 120 / 4 = 30 km in every 15 minutes, not 20 km, so statement III is wrong.

questions.q: Assertion (A): The speed of a city bus for a whole trip is usually given as an average speed. Reason (R): In everyday life, objects seldom move with a constant speed over long distances or for long intervals of time. Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: because the bus seldom keeps a constant speed for long, its speed for the trip can only be described as total distance divided by total time, the average speed.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: A rowing boat moves along a straight canal. The crew notes its position from markers on the bank every 5 minutes: 0 km at 6:00 am, 1.5 km at 6:05 am, 3.0 km at 6:10 am, 4.5 km at 6:15 am and 6.0 km at 6:20 am. (a) Find the distance covered in each 5-minute interval. (b) Is the boat in uniform or non-uniform linear motion? Give the reason. (c) Find its speed in km/h and in m/s.
questions.a: (a) 1.5 km in each of the four 5-minute intervals. (b) Uniform linear motion, because it covers equal distances in equal intervals of time along a straight line. (c) 6.0 km in 20 min = 1/3 h, so speed = 6.0 / (1/3) = 18 km/h = 18 x 1000 m / 3600 s = 5 m/s.
s: (a) 1.5 km in each interval
(b) Uniform: equal distances in equal intervals
(c) 18 km/h = 5 m/s

questions.q: Two drones fly along the same straight line from the same start. Their positions are noted every 10 s. Drone P: 0 m, 40 m, 80 m, 120 m, 160 m at 0, 10, 20, 30, 40 s. Drone Q: 0 m, 35 m, 90 m, 130 m, 180 m at the same times. (a) Find the distance each drone covers in each 10 s interval. (b) Which drone is in uniform linear motion? Give the reason. (c) Find the average speed of each drone over the 40 s in m/s. (d) A film crew needs a drone that moves at a steady speed for a smooth shot, and a courier needs the drone that covers 180 m in the least time. Which drone should each choose? Justify using your answers, taking P to keep its speed beyond 160 m.
questions.a: (a) P: 40 m, 40 m, 40 m, 40 m. Q: 35 m, 55 m, 40 m, 50 m. (b) Drone P, because it covers equal distances in equal intervals of time along a straight line; Q covers unequal distances in equal intervals, so its motion is non-uniform. (c) P: 160 m / 40 s = 4 m/s; Q: 180 m / 40 s = 4.5 m/s. (d) The film crew should choose P, since its speed stays constant at 4 m/s. The courier should choose Q: Q covers 180 m in 40 s, while P at 4 m/s needs 180 / 4 = 45 s. Uniform motion means a steady speed, not a higher one.
s: (b) P: equal distances in equal times
(c) P 4 m/s, Q 4.5 m/s
(d) Film crew P (steady); courier Q (40 s against 45 s)

questions.q: Two runners run a 4 km stretch of a marathon along a straight road. Runner A takes 6 min for each kilometre. Runner B takes 4 min for the first kilometre, 5 min for the second, 6 min for the third and 5 min for the fourth. (a) Find the total time each runner takes. (b) Find the average speed of each in km/h. (c) Whose motion is uniform? Give the reason. (d) Find B's speed in the kilometre in which he was fastest. (e) The coach says, 'A ran at a steady speed all the way, so A must have been faster than B over the 4 km.' Is the coach right? Justify.
questions.a: (a) A: 4 x 6 = 24 min; B: 4 + 5 + 6 + 5 = 20 min. (b) A: 4 km / (24/60 h) = 10 km/h; B: 4 km / (20/60 h) = 12 km/h. (c) A's motion is uniform: he covers equal distances (1 km) in equal times (6 min). B takes unequal times for equal distances, so his speed keeps changing and his motion is non-uniform. (d) First kilometre: 1 km in 4 min = 1 / (4/60) = 15 km/h. (e) No. Uniform motion means a constant speed, not a high one. B covered the same 4 km in less time, so B's average speed (12 km/h) is higher than A's (10 km/h).
s: (a) A 24 min, B 20 min
(b) A 10 km/h, B 12 km/h
(c) A uniform; B non-uniform, unequal times for equal distances
(d) 15 km/h in the first kilometre
(e) No: steady is not the same as fast; B's average 12 km/h beats A's 10 km/h
